question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, cognitive psychologist Ysolde Tennick claimed that drivers aged 65 to 80 who play an action video game for several weeks respond faster to road hazards than drivers of that age who play a word-puzzle game, because the action game enlarges the region of a scene they take in at a single glance.
• A team led by Bram Aldersey at the Thursby Mobility Lab assigned 30 drivers aged 65 to 80 to play an action game and 30 drivers of the same age range to play a word-puzzle game, each for 40 minutes a day over six weeks.
• Afterward, every driver completed the same driving simulator course, which contained 12 hazards such as a pedestrian stepping into the road.
• The team recorded the time from the appearance of each hazard to the driver's first press of the brake pedal; the average was 0.71 seconds for the action-game group and 0.89 seconds for the word-puzzle group.
• The same 60 drivers also completed a screen task. On each trial, a car shape was flashed briefly at the center of the screen while a target was flashed briefly at a point toward the screen's edge, and the driver had to name the car shape and then point to where the target had appeared.
• The team recorded the farthest distance from screen center, in degrees, at which a driver pointed to the target's location correctly; the average was 24 degrees for the action-game group and 24 degrees for the word-puzzle group.
• Drivers sat 60 centimeters from the screen with their chin on a rest, and each driver completed the simulator course and the screen task in a single visit.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Tennick's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Tennick's claim: the action-game group averaged 0.71 seconds to brake in the simulator, compared with an average of 0.89 seconds for the word-puzzle group.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Tennick's claim: the action-game group and the word-puzzle group averaged the same farthest distance of correct pointing on the screen task, 24 degrees.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Tennick's observation but not their explanation: the action-game group averaged 0.71 seconds to brake against the word-puzzle group's 0.89 seconds, yet the two groups averaged the same farthest distance of correct pointing on the screen task, 24 degrees.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Tennick's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the action-game group averaged 0.71 seconds to brake against the word-puzzle group's 0.89 seconds, and both groups averaged 24 degrees on the screen task.
explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it matches each part of Tennick's claim to the data that bears on it. Tennick's sentence says two things: that older drivers who play an action game respond faster to road hazards than those who play a word-puzzle game, and that this happens because the action game enlarges the region of a scene they take in at a single glance. The simulator braking times bear on the first part. The action-game group averaged 0.71 seconds from the appearance of a hazard to the first press of the brake, compared with 0.89 seconds for the word-puzzle group, so the faster response Tennick described did appear. The screen task bears on the second part. A driver who takes in a larger region of a scene at a single glance, while looking at the center, should be able to locate a target correctly at a greater distance from the center, so the farthest distance of correct pointing shows whether the region taken in differs between the groups. Both groups averaged 24 degrees, so there was no sign that the action-game group took in a larger region. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about seating distance, the chin rest, and completing both tasks in a single visit describe the method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 0.71 versus 0.89 seconds do fit the first part of Tennick's claim, that action-game players respond faster to hazards, but Tennick also said this happens because the game enlarges the region of a scene taken in at a glance, and the screen task results (24 degrees for both groups) show no such difference. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical averages on the screen task (24 degrees for both groups) do count against Tennick's explanation about the region of a scene taken in at a glance, but the claim also says that older drivers who play the action game respond faster to hazards, and the simulator braking times (0.71 versus 0.89 seconds) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the screen task result as a check on whether the groups were comparable rather than as a test of the explanation. The notes describe the task as a record of the farthest distance from screen center at which each driver located a briefly flashed target, which bears on how large a region of a scene a driver takes in at a glance, the very thing Tennick's 'because' clause is about. The identical averages (24 degrees) therefore show that the groups did not differ on that, which fails to support the explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the screen task as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.
